variants.name: Classic attorney: friend-declared gate with private forwarders and selected nested-type aliases
variants.idiom_name: friend-declared attorney with private static forwarders and public typedefs for selected private nested types (More C++ Idioms: Attorney-Client)
variants.implementation_notes: C++ friendship grants the friend every private and protected name in the grantor, and friendship is neither inherited nor transitive (cppreference, friend declaration). The classic attorney makes one gatekeeper the grantor's friend, keeps its forwarding functions private, and friends only the requestor with that gatekeeper; each static forwarder takes the client by reference and calls one selected operation. The type-oriented form also puts a public typedef such as `typedef Client::PrivateNode node_type;` in the attorney: the client friendship makes that lookup legal, while the requestor names `Attorney::node_type` without seeing other private nested types. This alias is intentionally public to every translation unit that includes the attorney header, so header placement and the nested type's own public API determine the remaining boundary. LLVM's SchedulerInternalsAttorney is a production example: it aliases Scheduler::BndlSchedState and provides narrow static accessors for unit tests. Prefer this over blanket friendship or a #define private public test hack; it is compile-time encapsulation, not runtime security.
pitfalls: Wrong move: make the forwarders public and distribute the attorney header everywhere; failure: every includer can call the full selected surface and any public nested-type alias, so the friend list no longer limits callers; instead: keep operations private, friend only the requestor, and ship the alias header only where that type is part of the contract.

Wrong move: hand-copy a forwarder's signature or expose a nested type whose public API is much larger than the intended grant; failure: signature drift silently changes calls, or the requestor gains more capability than the attorney review suggests; instead: forward exact signatures and use a purpose-built nested type or a passkey when the type itself is too broad.

Wrong move: assume friendship propagates through inheritance or another helper; failure: derived requestors and nested helpers cannot name the grantor's private members, or a direct friend is added as a bypass; instead: declare each intended attorney/requestor edge explicitly and remove parallel direct friends.

Wrong move: treat the alias as a pImpl firewall; failure: exposing Client::Node in a public typedef makes its declaration a header dependency and couples clients to implementation changes; instead: keep pImpl opaque and define the attorney in the privileged adapter or test boundary.
The attorney itself has full access: if one of its members is made public (or a public member is added later), the narrow grant silently widens to everything the attorney can reach in the client.

Forwarding signatures duplicate the client's private ones, so a change that still converts (int to double, a new default argument) compiles and forwards the wrong thing until a call site breaks - keep the attorney minimal or re-export the members instead of re-typing them.

Friendship is neither inherited nor transitive, which is usually what you want but surprises people who expect a derived requestor or a nested helper to inherit the grant; and the friend class cannot be distributed without the class that befriends it, so the coupling is real.

variants.name: Templated attorney: inherit the client and re-export chosen privates with using-declarations
variants.idiom_name: Attorney<TClient> : public TClient with using Client::member re-exports
variants.implementation_notes: A less repetitive realization (the variant the Approxion article adopts for test attorneys): template<class TClient> class Attorney : public TClient holds the reference and inherits the constructor (using Attorney<TClient>::Attorney), and a concrete ClientAttorney : public Attorney<Client> re-exports only the chosen private members with using Client::privateMethod; / using Client::values;. The client still declares the concrete attorney a friend, so the grant stays the same, but the forwarders are not typed by hand and therefore cannot drift out of sync when a signature changes. Prefer it when the attorney is a test utility that will be extended often; keep the classic forwarding class when the granted surface must be filtered or adapted rather than merely re-exposed.
pitfalls: Inheriting from the client to re-export members means the attorney is now a kind of Client (substitutable, sliced, destructible as a Client), which is too strong a relationship for what is only an access gate.

The using-declaration route still needs the friendship (the derived attorney cannot name inaccessible members otherwise) and exports whole members: it cannot narrow a parameter list, filter results or expose a computed view, so it fits test access better than production seams.
Inheriting constructors requires C++11, and a client with a deleted or protected destructor or a non-virtual public destructor makes the by-value attorney dangerous to delete polymorphically.
